questions.stem: A 46 year old man is on day 3 of an admission with severe acute pancreatitis. He becomes increasingly breathless. His pulse rate is 122 bpm, BP 104/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 85% breathing air. A chest X-ray shows bilateral diffuse infiltrates with a normal heart size. Investigations:

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Bilateral diffuse infiltrates with a normal heart size: ARDS.

questions.q: Which is the most likely interpretation of his arterial blood gas?
questions.e: PaO2 below 8 kPa with a normal or low PaCO2 is type 1 respiratory failure; ARDS after pancreatitis is a classic cause.

steps.x: ARDS after pancreatitis, a PaO2 of 6.8 kPa and a low PaCO2.

elim: The PaCO2 is low, not raised, and the pH is not acidaemic.
PaO2 is well below 8 kPa; anxiety alone does not cause hypoxaemia.
The pH is not low and the bicarbonate is normal.
Type 2 needs PaCO2 above 6 kPa; his is low.

steps.x: D: Type 1 respiratory failure. PaO2 <8 kPa with normal or low PaCO2 = type 1 (oxygenation failure). ARDS, pneumonia, pulmonary oedema and PE cause it.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman has 5 days of ascending leg weakness that began 2 weeks after a diarrhoeal illness. She now has a weak cough and can count to only 8 in one breath. Reflexes are absent in all four limbs. Her pulse rate is 104 bpm, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89% breathing air. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely interpretation of her arterial blood gas?
questions.e: Guillain-Barré syndrome weakens the respiratory muscles, so she cannot ventilate enough: hypoxaemia with PaCO2 above 6 kPa is type 2 respiratory failure.

steps.x: Neuromuscular weakness with a low PaO2 and a raised PaCO2.

elim: The bicarbonate is normal; the acidosis is from the raised PaCO2.
The pH is low, not high.
PaO2 is below 8 kPa and PaCO2 is above 6 kPa.
Type 1 has a normal or low PaCO2; hers is raised.

steps.x: E: Type 2 respiratory failure. PaO2 <8 kPa plus PaCO2 >6 kPa = type 2 (hypercapnic). Neuromuscular disease is a cause.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man with COPD is admitted with 4 days of worsening breathlessness and purulent sputum. He is drowsy, with warm peripheries, a bounding pulse and a coarse flapping tremor of the outstretched hands. He has no jaundice or spider naevi. His pulse rate is 108 bpm, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 84% breathing air. Capillary glucose is 6.4 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his tremor?
questions.e: Asterixis with warm peripheries, a bounding pulse and drowsiness in an exacerbation of COPD are signs of CO2 retention (type 2 respiratory failure).

steps.x: COPD exacerbation plus CO2 retention signs: flap, bounding pulse, warm hands, drowsiness.

elim: No jaundice or stigmata of liver disease; COPD with hypercapnic signs fits better.
His capillary glucose is normal.
Beta-agonists cause a fine tremor, not a coarse flap with drowsiness.
Nothing suggests kidney failure; the setting is a COPD exacerbation with CO2 retention signs.

steps.x: C: Raised arterial carbon dioxide. Asterixis in a breathless COPD patient = CO2 retention until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: An 84 year old woman in a care home has 3 days of cough and fever and has become acutely confused and drowsy today. Her lips are blue and she has crackles at the right base. Her temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 116 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 83% breathing air. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her confusion?
questions.e: Pneumonia has caused severe hypoxaemia with a low PaCO2 (type 1 respiratory failure); altered mental state and cyanosis mark it as severe.

steps.x: Pneumonia, cyanosis, confusion and a PaO2 of 6.6 kPa with a low PaCO2.

elim: Dementia develops over months to years, not in one day with hypoxaemia.
Nothing points to low glucose; she is severely hypoxaemic.
No head injury or focal signs, and her ABG explains the confusion.
The source is the chest, and the hypoxaemia itself causes the altered mental state.

steps.x: D: Type 1 respiratory failure. Confusion, drowsiness and cyanosis are signs of respiratory failure; altered mental state means it is severe.

questions.stem: A 73 year old man is 1 day after a total hip replacement and has a morphine patient-controlled analgesia pump. A nurse finds him difficult to rouse. His pupils are pinpoint. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 62 bpm, BP 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 7 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 86% breathing air. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Morphine suppresses respiratory drive, causing hypoventilation with a raised PaCO2: type 2 respiratory failure from opioid toxicity.

steps.x: Opioid PCA, pinpoint pupils, slow breathing and a raised PaCO2.

elim: Causes type 1 failure with petechiae and confusion, not pinpoint pupils and a slow respiratory rate.
No fever, and it would raise the respiratory rate, not slow it.
Does not cause pinpoint pupils, bradypnoea or a raised PaCO2.
Causes tachypnoea and type 1 failure with a low PaCO2.

steps.x: C: Opioid-induced type 2 respiratory failure. Opioids reduce respiratory drive and cause type 2 respiratory failure; slow breathing plus hypercapnia.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman who takes the combined oral contraceptive pill has sudden right pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness. Her pulse rate is 118 bpm, BP 122/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89% breathing air. Her chest is clear. Investigations:
questions.q: Which best describes her arterial blood gas?
o: Type 1 respiratory failure with respiratory alkalosis
questions.e: PE causes hypoxaemia with a low PaCO2 from tachypnoea: type 1 respiratory failure, here with a respiratory alkalosis.

steps.x: Likely PE: PaO2 7.3 kPa with a low PaCO2 and high pH.

elim: Her pH is high and PaCO2 low.
The bicarbonate is normal; the alkalosis is from hyperventilation.
A PaO2 of 7.3 kPa is markedly low.
PaCO2 is low, not above 6 kPa.

steps.x: D: Type 1 respiratory failure with respiratory alkalosis. PE is a cause of type 1 respiratory failure; hyperventilation lowers PaCO2.

questions.stem: A 71 year old woman with severe COPD attends the respiratory clinic for review. She is at her usual baseline, with breathlessness after 50 metres. She is alert and has no flap. Her pulse rate is 84 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 88% breathing air. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely interpretation of her arterial blood gas?
o: Chronic type 2 respiratory failure with metabolic compensation
questions.e: Low PaO2 and raised PaCO2 with a normal pH and high bicarbonate means chronic, compensated type 2 respiratory failure, typical of a stable CO2 retainer with COPD.

steps.x: Stable COPD, PaCO2 6.9 kPa, normal pH, bicarbonate 33.

elim: In acute failure the pH is low because the kidneys have not yet retained bicarbonate.
The raised bicarbonate is compensating for a raised PaCO2; the pH is normal.
PaO2 is below 8 kPa and PaCO2 is above 6 kPa.
PaCO2 is raised, so this is type 2.

steps.x: B: Chronic type 2 respiratory failure with metabolic compensation. Raised PaCO2 with a normal pH and raised bicarbonate = chronic type 2 failure; a low pH means acute.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man with COPD has 3 days of increasing breathlessness, wheeze and green sputum. He is tired and using accessory muscles. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 146/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 85% breathing air. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: An infective COPD exacerbation with PaO2 below 8 kPa, PaCO2 above 6 kPa and acidaemia is acute type 2 respiratory failure, the most important cause of which is COPD.

steps.x: COPD exacerbation: PaCO2 8.1 kPa with pH 7.29.

elim: The pH is low, so the kidneys have not compensated: this is acute.
The bicarbonate is normal; the acidosis is respiratory.
Usually gives type 1 failure with a low PaCO2, without purulent sputum.
PaCO2 is above 6 kPa.

steps.x: A: Acute type 2 respiratory failure. COPD is the most important cause of type 2 respiratory failure; acidaemia means it is acute.

questions.stem: A 59 year old woman has 2 days of fever, rigors and a productive cough. She has bronchial breathing at the right base. Her temperature is 39.1°C, pulse rate 112 bpm, BP 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 88% breathing air. Her arterial gas shows PaO2 7.2 kPa and PaCO2 4.3 kPa. A chest X-ray is taken.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her respiratory failure?
questions.e: Fever, bronchial breathing and lobar consolidation with type 1 respiratory failure point to pneumonia; the other options cause type 2 failure.

clues: fever, rigors and a productive cough
steps.x: Infective symptoms, consolidation, and a low PaO2 with normal PaCO2 (type 1).

elim: A neuromuscular cause of type 2 failure; she has fever and consolidation.
Gives chronic type 2 failure with weakness, not fever and consolidation.
Causes type 2 failure from muscle weakness, with a raised PaCO2.
Causes slow breathing and type 2 failure with a raised PaCO2.

steps.x: E: Pneumonia. Pneumonia is a classic cause of type 1 respiratory failure; neuromuscular disease and opioids cause type 2.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man has 4 days of fever and cough. He is breathless at rest and speaks in short sentences. His temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 128/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 82% breathing air. An arterial gas shows PaO2 6.4 kPa and PaCO2 4.0 kPa.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
questions.e: Saturations of 82% mean marked desaturated haemoglobin, so central cyanosis is expected; asterixis needs CO2 retention, which he does not have.

steps.x: Severe hypoxaemia with a low PaCO2: type 1 failure.

elim: A sign of CO2 retention; his PaCO2 is low.
Develops over months; not caused by acute hypoxaemia.
Can occur with chronic severe hypercapnia, not acute type 1 failure.
A feature of chronic obstructive disease, not acute pneumonia.

steps.x: B: Central cyanosis. Cyanosis, tachypnoea, breathlessness and confusion are features of respiratory failure; asterixis is specific to CO2 retention.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman is on the ward with pneumonia. Overnight she becomes more breathless and fatigued. She is now acutely confused and does not know where she is. Her pulse rate is 118 bpm, BP 116/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 86% on 4 L/min oxygen. She has a productive cough and expiratory wheeze.
questions.q: Which finding most strongly indicates that her respiratory failure is severe?
questions.e: An altered mental state shows the brain is affected by hypoxaemia or hypercapnia and marks severe respiratory failure needing urgent escalation.

clues: acutely confused and does not know where she is
steps.x: Hypoxaemic despite oxygen, and now confused.

elim: Common in chest infections and does not by itself mark severity.
A general feature of respiratory failure, not a marker of severity.
Reflects the infection, not the severity of gas exchange failure.
Tachycardia is common with fever and hypoxaemia; altered mental state is the red flag.

steps.x: A: Acute confusion. Severe respiratory failure shows altered mental state: confusion and drowsiness.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man with COPD is breathless and drowsy on the ward 2 days after a laparotomy. Pulse oximetry shows oxygen saturation 87% breathing air. His pulse rate is 104 bpm, BP 136/80 mmHg and respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute. The doctor needs to know whether he is retaining carbon dioxide.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: The ABG is the gold standard: it measures PaO2, PaCO2 and pH, which classify type 1 versus type 2 failure and its severity.

steps.x: Pulse oximetry shows hypoxaemia but cannot show CO2 or pH.

elim: Helps find the cause but cannot measure PaCO2 or pH.
Measures airflow obstruction, not gas exchange.
Not used acutely and does not measure blood gases.
Gives pH and a rough CO2 but not an accurate PaO2 to classify respiratory failure.

steps.x: A: Arterial blood gas. ABG is the gold standard for respiratory failure: PaO2, PaCO2 and pH.

questions.stem: A 41 year old woman with known myasthenia gravis has 2 days of worsening weakness, difficulty swallowing and breathlessness after starting a course of antibiotics. Her speech is nasal and her cough is weak. Her pulse rate is 110 bpm, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute with shallow breaths and oxygen saturation 90% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on arterial blood gas?
questions.e: Myasthenic crisis weakens the respiratory muscles, causing acute hypoventilation: low PaO2, raised PaCO2 and acidosis (acute type 2 failure).

steps.x: Respiratory muscle weakness: she cannot clear CO2, and it has happened over 2 days.

elim: A normal gas; she is hypoxaemic on oximetry and hypoventilating.
Type 1 failure with hyperventilation, as in PE or pneumonia.
Chronic compensated pattern; her deterioration is acute so pH will be low.
Metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation; she is hypoventilating, so PaCO2 will be high.

steps.x: B: pH 7.28, PaO2 7.6 kPa, PaCO2 7.9 kPa. Neuromuscular disease causes type 2 failure; an acute rise in PaCO2 gives acidosis.

questions.stem: A 78 year old man has 2 days of cough and breathlessness. He has coarse crackles at the left base. His temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 89% breathing air. An arterial gas confirms type 1 respiratory failure. He is started on oxygen.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial imaging to identify the cause?
questions.e: Once the ABG confirms respiratory failure, a chest X-ray (with bloods) is the first-line test to find the underlying cause.

clues: coarse crackles at the left base
steps.x: Type 1 failure confirmed; likely pneumonia.

elim: For suspected PE; here the features point to infection.
For heart failure; it would not show consolidation.
For interstitial lung disease, not a first-line test.
Not used to find the cause of acute respiratory failure.

steps.x: E: Plain chest radiograph. Find the cause first-line with a chest X-ray and blood tests.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman wakes acutely breathless with central chest tightness for 1 hour. She has bibasal crackles. Her pulse rate is 112 bpm, BP 158/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 86% breathing air. ABG shows type 1 respiratory failure and chest X-ray shows bilateral pulmonary oedema.
questions.q: Which additional investigation is most appropriate to look for the cause?
questions.e: Chest tightness with acute pulmonary oedema suggests myocardial infarction; an ECG is the additional test to find the cause, with CT reserved for suspected PE.

steps.x: Pulmonary oedema with chest tightness: look for ischaemia.

elim: Considered if PE is suspected; this is pulmonary oedema.
Used to rule out PE; it will not show the cause of pulmonary oedema.
Not useful in acute respiratory failure.
For infection; there is no fever or purulent sputum.

steps.x: C: Electrocardiogram. ECG is an additional test in respiratory failure; CT only if PE is suspected.

questions.stem: A 47 year old man is 6 days after an anterior resection of the rectum. He has sudden breathlessness. His chest is clear. His pulse rate is 124 bpm, BP 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 88% breathing air. ABG shows PaO2 7.6 kPa and PaCO2 3.9 kPa. His chest X-ray is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to identify the cause?
questions.e: Postoperative type 1 failure with a clear chest and normal X-ray suggests PE, so CT (CTPA) is the test.

steps.x: Recent surgery, sudden breathlessness, type 1 failure, normal X-ray.

elim: Invasive and not used to look for a clot.
May show right heart strain but does not confirm a PE.
Already normal; it cannot show a pulmonary embolus.
No features of infection.

steps.x: B: CT pulmonary angiogram. Hypoxaemia with a clear chest X-ray after surgery = think PE: CTPA.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman with an exacerbation of COPD was started on bilevel non-invasive ventilation 1 hour ago for an arterial pH of 7.29 and PaCO2 of 8.2 kPa. She is tolerating the mask. Her pulse rate is 100 bpm, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 90% on 2 L/min entrained oxygen.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to assess her response?
questions.e: Response to NIV is judged on repeat ABG (pH and PaCO2) plus clinical status, usually at 1 hour.

steps.x: She is on NIV for acidotic type 2 failure; the aim is to lower PaCO2.

elim: Does not measure whether her PaCO2 and pH are improving.
Not useful on NIV and does not measure CO2.
Shows oxygenation but not the PaCO2 or pH that NIV is treating.
Not used during an acute exacerbation.

steps.x: D: Repeat arterial blood gas. Monitor with repeat ABG and clinical status.

questions.stem: A 39 year old man with no lung disease has 3 days of fever and cough and is now confused and very breathless. His temperature is 39.0°C, pulse rate 126 bpm, BP 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 81% breathing air. Blood has been taken for an arterial gas.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Wait for the arterial gas result
questions.e: He is confused and severely hypoxaemic with no CO2 retention risk, so give oxygen immediately and titrate to 94–98%.

steps.x: Severe hypoxaemia, confusion, no risk of CO2 retention.

elim: An escalation if he fails to respond; oxygen comes first.
No features of pulmonary oedema.
Used for acidotic type 2 failure, not as the first step here.
Breathlessness, confusion and hypoxaemia need immediate oxygen.

steps.x: D: Oxygen 15 L/min via non-rebreather mask. Breathlessness plus confusion plus hypoxaemia = immediate oxygen; target 94–98% in most patients.

questions.stem: A 62 year old man with motor neurone disease is admitted with a chest infection. He has weak respiratory muscles and an ABG last month showed a PaCO2 of 6.7 kPa. His pulse rate is 98 bpm, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 86% breathing air. He is alert.
questions.q: Which oxygen saturation target should be prescribed?
questions.e: Neuromuscular disease with a raised PaCO2 puts him at risk of CO2 retention, so the target is 88–92%, as in COPD.

steps.x: A neuromuscular patient who already retains CO2.

elim: Below the recommended target; this risks harmful hypoxaemia.
Not a standard BTS target range.
The target for most patients, not those at risk of CO2 retention.
Too high for anyone, and dangerous in a CO2 retainer.

steps.x: B: 88–92%. 88–92% applies to COPD AND anyone at risk of CO2 retention (neuromuscular, chest wall, obesity).

questions.stem: A 79 year old woman with heart failure has worsening breathlessness and orthopnoea. She has bibasal crackles, a raised JVP and pitting oedema to the knees. Her pulse rate is 104 bpm, BP 152/90 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 87% breathing air. ABG shows type 1 respiratory failure. She has been given oxygen.

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Cardiomegaly, pulmonary oedema and small bilateral effusions.

questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: Treat the underlying cause: pulmonary oedema needs a diuretic.

steps.x: Type 1 failure from pulmonary oedema.

elim: For infection; there is no fever or consolidation.
For PE; this is fluid overload.
For bronchospasm; it does not treat pulmonary oedema.
Bilevel NIV is for acidotic type 2 failure; treat the cause first.

steps.x: B: Intravenous furosemide. Oxygen plus treat the cause: diuretics for pulmonary oedema, antibiotics for infection, anticoagulation for PE.

questions.stem: A 56 year old man has a CT pulmonary angiogram that shows bilateral segmental pulmonary emboli. He has no right ventricular strain. On 2 L/min of oxygen, his pulse rate is 98 bpm, BP 134/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95%. He has no history of bleeding.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: Treat the underlying cause of his type 1 failure: anticoagulate a stable PE.

steps.x: Stable PE causing hypoxaemia, now on oxygen at target.

elim: Only if anticoagulation is contraindicated.
For pulmonary oedema, not PE.
Only for massive PE when thrombolysis fails or is contraindicated; he is stable.
Reserved for massive PE with haemodynamic compromise; he is stable.

steps.x: C: Oral anticoagulation with apixaban. Respiratory failure from PE: oxygen plus anticoagulation; thrombolysis only if haemodynamically unstable.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man with an exacerbation of COPD has had nebulised bronchodilators, oral prednisolone and doxycycline. On 28% Venturi oxygen his pulse rate is 96 bpm, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 90%. He is alert. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Change to 15 L/min oxygen via non-rebreather mask
Continue controlled oxygen and medical treatment
questions.e: His PaCO2 is raised but the pH is normal (compensated), so NIV is not indicated; continue 88–92% oxygen and treatment.

steps.x: Saturations on target, raised PaCO2, but pH 7.38.

elim: Raises the risk of worsening hypercapnia; his saturations are on target.
A respiratory stimulant only when NIV is not available or appropriate.
For failure of NIV; he is alert with a normal pH.
Indicated for pH 7.25–7.35; his pH is normal.

steps.x: B: Continue controlled oxygen and medical treatment. NIV is for type 2 failure with acidosis (pH 7.25–7.35), not a raised PaCO2 alone.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman with COPD has had back-to-back nebulised salbutamol, ipratropium, oral prednisolone and amoxicillin for an exacerbation. One hour later on 24% Venturi oxygen she is tired but rousable. Her respiratory rate is 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 90%. Investigations:

visual.title: Arterial pH
visual.label: pH 7.28
visual.caption: pH 7.25–7.35 with a raised PaCO2 is the NIV range.

questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Persistent type 2 failure with pH 7.25–7.35 despite full medical treatment is the indication for NIV (BiPAP).

steps.x: Acidotic type 2 failure despite maximal medical therapy.

elim: CPAP does not augment tidal volume, so it does not clear CO2.
Will worsen hypercapnia in a CO2 retainer.
A third-line bronchodilator; it does not treat persistent acidotic hypercapnia.
For those who fail NIV or with pH well below 7.25.

steps.x: E: Non-invasive ventilation (BiPAP). pH 7.25–7.35 with raised PaCO2 in COPD = bilevel NIV.

questions.stem: A 28 year old man with Guillain-Barré syndrome is on the neurology ward. Over 6 hours he has become unable to clear his secretions and is pooling saliva. He is drowsy. His pulse rate is 122 bpm, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute with shallow breaths and oxygen saturation 87% on 4 L/min oxygen. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Severe, worsening type 2 failure with drowsiness and an unprotected airway needs intubation and mechanical ventilation.

steps.x: Neuromuscular type 2 failure, falling consciousness, cannot protect airway.

elim: Unsafe with bulbar weakness and pooling secretions, and he is deteriorating fast.
Does not correct hypoventilation or protect the airway.
Treats the disease but not the immediate respiratory failure.
There is no bronchospasm.

steps.x: D: Intubation and mechanical ventilation. Severe failure, or failure of NIV: intubate and ventilate.

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman with COPD is brought to the emergency department very breathless and confused. Her pulse rate is 114 bpm, BP 150/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 78% breathing air. Her daughter says she has had high carbon dioxide levels before. An arterial sample has been sent.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: No oxygen until the arterial gas result
Oxygen via non-rebreather mask at 15 L/min
questions.e: Confusion with severe hypoxaemia needs immediate oxygen; in a known CO2 retainer give controlled oxygen targeting 88–92%.

steps.x: Severe hypoxaemia, confusion, known CO2 retainer.

elim: Escalation only after controlled oxygen, medical treatment and NIV fail.
Withholding oxygen from a hypoxaemic, confused patient is dangerous.
Needs the ABG to show pH 7.25–7.35 first.
Uncontrolled high-flow oxygen risks worsening hypercapnia.

steps.x: D: Oxygen via 28% Venturi mask now. Never withhold oxygen; in CO2 retainers give controlled oxygen to 88–92%.

questions.stem: A 49 year old woman has right lower lobe pneumonia. Her respiratory rate is 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 87% breathing air. Her arterial gas shows PaO2 7.1 kPa and PaCO2 4.4 kPa. A student asks why the oxygen is low.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her hypoxaemia?
questions.e: Consolidated alveoli are perfused but not ventilated (V/Q mismatch), so oxygen transfer falls while CO2 is still cleared.

steps.x: Type 1 failure from consolidation.

elim: Would raise PaCO2; hers is low.
She is breathing room air at sea level.
Anaemia lowers oxygen content, not PaO2.
Causes hypoventilation and a raised PaCO2.

steps.x: E: Ventilation–perfusion mismatch. Type 1 = V/Q mismatch or diffusion impairment; CO2 diffuses more readily so it stays normal or low.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man with motor neurone disease has morning headaches and daytime sleepiness. His lungs are clear on examination and his chest X-ray is normal. His respiratory rate is 22 breaths per minute with shallow breaths. Investigations:
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his raised PaCO2?
o: Diffusion impairment across a thickened membrane
Reduced minute ventilation from respiratory muscle weakness
questions.e: Weak respiratory muscles reduce minute ventilation, so CO2 is not cleared: alveolar hypoventilation causes type 2 failure.

steps.x: Neuromuscular weakness with normal lungs.

elim: Lowers PaO2 but CO2 still diffuses well, and his lungs are clear.
Seen in fever or sepsis; not the problem in MND.
Causes hypoxaemia with a normal PaCO2.
His X-ray is normal; V/Q mismatch gives type 1 failure.

steps.x: C: Reduced minute ventilation from respiratory muscle weakness. Type 2 = alveolar hypoventilation: low drive, muscle weakness, or high airway resistance/dead space (COPD).

questions.stem: A 69 year old man with severe COPD has a chronically raised PaCO2 of 7.0 kPa and bicarbonate of 34 mmol/L when stable. He is admitted with an exacerbation and prescribed oxygen with a target saturation of 88–92%. A nursing student asks why the target is lower than for other patients.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Oxygen toxicity damages the alveoli within minutes
Partial reliance on hypoxic drive to breathe
questions.e: Chronic CO2 retainers rely partly on hypoxic drive; uncontrolled high-flow oxygen can suppress ventilation and worsen hypercapnia, hence 88–92%.

steps.x: A chronic CO2 retainer with renal compensation.

elim: Oxygen does not constrict the airways.
Oxygen does not raise metabolic CO2 production.
Not the reason for the target.
Toxicity needs very prolonged high concentrations.

steps.x: E: Partial reliance on hypoxic drive to breathe. Hypoxic drive in chronic CO2 retainers is why the target is 88–92%.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman with an exacerbation of COPD and an arterial pH of 7.30 is started on bilevel non-invasive ventilation with an inspiratory pressure of 15 cmH2O and expiratory pressure of 5 cmH2O. After 1 hour her PaCO2 has fallen from 8.6 to 7.4 kPa.

visual.title: On bilevel NIV
visual.caption: PaCO2 falls as tidal volume increases.

questions.q: Which is the main mechanism by which the inspiratory pressure lowers her PaCO2?
o: Greater tidal volume, raising alveolar ventilation
questions.e: Inspiratory positive pressure (IPAP) boosts tidal volume to clear CO2, while expiratory pressure (EPAP) keeps alveoli open.

clues: PaCO2 has fallen from 8.6 to 7.4 kPa
steps.x: Bilevel NIV: IPAP and EPAP have different roles.

elim: Oxygen is entrained separately and does not clear CO2.
That is the role of the expiratory pressure (EPAP).
NIV does not change metabolic CO2 production.
Positive pressure is not a bronchodilator.

steps.x: C: Greater tidal volume, raising alveolar ventilation. IPAP augments tidal volume (clears CO2); EPAP keeps alveoli open.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man with COPD has an arterial PaCO2 of 9.1 kPa during an exacerbation. He is drowsy and has a coarse flapping tremor when he holds his arms out with wrists extended. His liver function tests and capillary glucose are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his tremor?
o: Metabolic encephalopathy from carbon dioxide retention
questions.e: CO2 retention causes a metabolic encephalopathy affecting the reticular activating system and motor pathways, giving asterixis and drowsiness.

clues: liver function tests and capillary glucose are normal
steps.x: High CO2, drowsy, flap, no liver disease.

elim: Gives a fine tremor, not a flap with drowsiness.
Causes intention tremor and ataxia.
Causes tetany and carpopedal spasm, not asterixis.
Causes sensory loss and weakness, not a flap.

steps.x: D: Metabolic encephalopathy from carbon dioxide retention. Asterixis in hypercapnia is a metabolic encephalopathy.
